excerpt_original: How James Clifford Kent avoids the obvious tropes to make unexpected pictures of the much-photographed island nation. L’article A Fresh View of Cuba est apparu en premier sur Blind Magazine .

blocks.text: Recently, I got my hands on a zine featuring the work of the wonderful London-based photographer James Clifford Kent. It’s called Till the Bitter End — published and designed by Malak Kabbani — and it’s gorgeous, moving, and incredibly well done. The word “zine” can carry low-rent connotations, but the entire experience, from the quality of the images and design to the risograph printing to the paper itself, plays like a high-quality book. Making photo books has become both difficult & expensive, and the photo world clearly needs a new option; to my eye, Kent and Kabbani have nailed it.

Kent shot this work in Cuba. If you hear yourself asking, “Do we really need another Cuba book?” the answer is Yes, and we need this one . There’s a combination of intimacy and surprise at work in Kent’s black-and-white images that is quite rare. Over the past two decades, he’s made 20-plus trips to Cuba — and you feel that connection in every grainy, moody, unexpected picture.

blocks.text: “I first arrived in Havana in 2004, aged 20, and taught at the Universidad de La Habana,” Kent told me. “On my first day, I walked into a dark classroom during a blackout and found students dancing. It was such a vibe and I fell in love right there and then.” Before he left for Cuba, his mother gave him a camera “so I could send photos home and prove I was still alive.” He didn’t expect Mom’s camera to become his way of connecting with people. “Early on I spent many months in Cabaiguán, a sleepy town, with a group who became a sort-of adoptive family. I became the family photographer, taking pictures of birthdays, weddings, quinceañeras . They nicknamed me ‘Yuma’ — slang used for foreigners — and over time I became their Yuma.”

Kent told me that he quickly realized “how easy it is to rely on the exoticism of a foreign place,” but that that never interested him about Cuba. “I’m always trying to go beyond the spectacle and look for stories and feeling. If you can’t feel what’s in front of you, you can’t expect anyone else to.”

blocks.text: So there he is in a small town in Cuba with a camera he hadn’t had much practice with and an eye that wasn’t trained. How did he get from there to making these layered, revealing, often complicated frames? “I wanted to get better at taking pictures but had no visual references,” he told me. “So I began studying books full of photographs from the Revolution — monochrome pictures of rebels looking like rock stars. That imprinted on my way of seeing with the camera.” Later, with time, and with the help of his friend and mentor, the great Raúl Cañibano, he learned he could tell different stories in a single image. “I’m drawn to complex images,” Kent says. “Layers upon layers, where you feel you could scrub the surface and find more things underneath. Those are the pictures that reveal something new each time you look at them.”

When I asked Kent, now 42, how he knows when to press the shutter, he said this: “There’s always some element of luck, at least with the pictures I’m interested in. But my dad always said, You make your own luck. You know, you have to be in the room to make the picture.” And then Kent added something that I love and that explains so much about how he identifies moments: “It’s a kind of an instinctive recognition that several things have aligned: a gesture, a look, an unexpected detail, a relationship between things that might otherwise go unnoticed,” he says. “I feel the picture before I can explain it, usually through a tension or a contradiction I know won’t last.”
